author: high
claim: A maximal trail in a finite graph whose vertices all have even degree, when started at a vertex incident with an edge, must return to its initial vertex.
evidence: Let the trail start at s and suppose it stops at t distinct from s. At t, every visit before the final arrival consumes incident edges in entering/leaving pairs, while the final arrival consumes one further incident edge. Hence the number of trail edges incident with t is odd. Since deg(t) is even, the number of unused incident edges at t is odd and therefore positive, contradicting maximality.

links.statement: A maximal trail in an even-degree finite graph is closed.

glossary.s: the initial vertex of the maximal trail
glossary.t: the terminal vertex of the maximal trail distinct from s

author: high
claim: Deleting the edges of a closed trail from an even-degree graph leaves a residual graph in which every vertex still has even degree.
evidence: At each vertex, the occurrences of that vertex along a closed trail pair each arrival with a departure, including the cyclic pairing at the initial vertex. Thus the closed trail uses an even number of edges incident with each vertex. Subtracting this even number from the original even degree leaves an even residual degree.

links.statement: Closed-trail edge deletion preserves even degrees.

author: high
claim: In a connected graph, every nonempty edge-component remaining after deleting the edges of a nonempty closed trail shares a vertex with that trail.
evidence: Take a residual vertex incident with an edge and an original-graph path from it to the closed trail. At the first vertex of the path lying on the trail, the preceding path edge has its other endpoint off the trail. Hence that path edge cannot be one of the deleted trail edges, whose two endpoints both lie on the trail. It remains in the residual graph and shows that the residual component meets a trail vertex.

links.statement: Every residual edge-component attaches to the deleted closed trail.
